study.title: Map of Pitch
study.question: How does the treble staff show pitch?
study.passage:
Treble staff guide (written for this lesson):
Lines from bottom to top: E, G, B, D, F. Memory aid: "Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit."
Spaces from bottom to top: F, A, C, E, which spell FACE.
The treble clef curls around the second line, G, which is why it's also called the G clef.
Middle C sits on a ledger line just below the staff. D sits in the space below the bottom line. G and A above the staff use the space and a ledger line.
Activities: 1. Hand staff: hold up your left hand sideways; your five fingers are lines and the gaps are spaces. Point to notes as a partner calls names. 2. Note race: in teams, name 20 flash-card notes as fast as possible. 3. Word spelling: decode words written in notes (BAG, CAGE, FACE, BEAD, EGG). 4. Write your own note-word for a partner.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; staff names follow standard notation.

body.objective: Students will be able to describe step, skip and leap.
body.iCan: I can describe step, skip and leap.
successCriteria: I can identify steps, skips and leaps on the staff

body.hook: Sing "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" and trace the tune with your hand. It jumps up, then walks down step by step. Every melody has a shape, and musicians describe that shape with three words: step, skip and leap.

vocabulary.definition: A sequence of pitches that makes a tune.
Moving to the next line or space (next letter name).
Moving from a line to the next line, or a space to the next space (skipping one note).
A move larger than a skip.
The overall shape of a melody: rising, falling, arched or wave-like.

study.title: Melody Shapes
study.question: How do steps, skips and leaps shape a melody?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Body pitch (5 minutes): Sing "do-re-mi" up and down, touching knees, waist, shoulders and head to show pitch rising.
2. On the staff (10 minutes): Step = line to space or space to line (C to D). Skip = line to line or space to space (C to E). Leap = anything bigger (C to G). Label 12 intervals on a worksheet as S, K or L.
3. Contour drawing (10 minutes): Listen to four melodies and draw their shape as a line: "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" (leap up, then steps down); "Ode to Joy" from Beethoven's Symphony No. 9 (1824) (mostly steps); the opening of "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" (a large leap up); "Mary Had a Little Lamb" (steps and repeated notes).
4. Ear test (10 minutes): The teacher plays two notes; students show a flat hand (repeated), small move (step), two fingers (skip) or a big arm sweep (leap).
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; melodies named are traditional or widely known.

body.hook: Reading music becomes real when you play it. Today you put rhythm and pitch together on a classroom instrument and turn black dots on a page into a tune people can recognize.

study.title: Read and Play
study.question: How do I combine pitch and rhythm to play a melody?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
Instruments: keyboard, xylophone, recorder or boomwhackers (whatever is available).
1. Set up (5 minutes): Find C D E F G on your instrument and label them with stickers if needed.
2. Read before playing (5 minutes): For the melody "Ode to Joy" (opening, in C: E E F G | G F E D | C C D E | E. D D), first clap the rhythm, then say the note names in rhythm, then play.
3. Practice strategies (15 minutes): Slow first (half speed); chunking (one phrase at a time); loop the tricky bar three times correctly; then connect the phrases.
4. Second melody (10 minutes): "Hot Cross Buns" or "Mary Had a Little Lamb" using E D C. Partners play it for each other and check pitch and rhythm.
5. Share (5 minutes): Volunteers play one phrase for the class.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; Ode to Joy is from Beethoven's Symphony No. 9 (1824), public domain.
